Abuelo's Awakening: Trap rare — 50.1% with a negative IWD and only a quarter play rate means it rarely does anything. You need a real artifact or enchantment already in the yard and five-plus mana to make a flying body; in a format where craft cards want to stay on the battlefield, that setup mostly doesn't exist. Leave it in the sideboard.
Acrobatic Leap: Filler trick, 23rd card. The 55.4% is borrowed from the WU tempo decks that play it; a -0.2 IWD and 16.7% play rate say it does nothing on its own. The untap-plus-flying blowout is real, but you wheel it — never maindeck more than one.
Adaptive Gemguard: Filler body. 53.8% GIH with negative IWD says the 3/3 is the whole card — the pump taps two permanents at sorcery speed, so you're never both attacking and growing. Fine 23rd card in WU/RW artifact builds, never a card you move in on.
Attentive Sunscribe: Solid playable, better than a vanilla 2/2 in the decks that want it: it's an artifact body for UR/WU craft counts and the scry fires on attacks, not just tapper tricks. Negative IWD and the high OH split say it's a curve-filler you want early, never a card to draw late.
Bat Colony: Archetype-conditional role-player, not a slam. The 54.1% is conditioned on actually having 5-7 caves — a 27.3% play rate says most white decks correctly cut it. Note the gd_wr/oh_wr gap: it's a mid-game value engine, dead in an opener with two Plains.
Clay-Fired Bricks: Top-tier white pick and the poster child for craft done right: a two-drop that fixes, gains 2, feeds artifact counts, then becomes a wide-pump finisher when the game goes long. 60.2% with an ALSA of 3 — the rare white card that answers 'white can't win late.' Take it in any W deck, WU/RW especially.
Cosmium Blast: Solid playable, not premium — 4 damage at instant speed kills nearly anything, but the combat-only restriction means it never breaks a stall on your terms and +0.0 IWD says it's replacement-level. Fine 20th-23rd card in any white deck; take Sawblades or Petrify over it every time.
Dauntless Dismantler: Role-player with a real sideboard spike. A 1/4 for two blanks the RW/UR aggro starts this format punishes you for ignoring, and the tax on opposing artifacts is live against Izzet artifact decks. 54.0% with a negative IWD says filler-plus, not a pick you prioritize.
Deconstruction Hammer: Role-player, and only in a committed aggro shell. The negative IWD says it adds nothing to a random deck — it's a one-mana curve filler whose upside is that LCI is drowning in artifacts, so the sacrifice mode is almost always live. RW/WU aggro only.
Dusk Rose Reliquary: Premium removal at one mana — the additional cost is nearly free in a format swimming in Map tokens, craft leftovers and artifact chaff. 57.9% GIH with 85% play confirms it. Only real risk is casting it with no spare permanent; hold a Map for it.
Envoy of Okinec Ahau: Filler. A vanilla 3/3 for three with a mana sink so expensive it almost never fires, and the 39.5% play rate plus negative IWD say drafters were right to cut it. Last-playable body in a white deck that already gave up on being aggressive.
Fabrication Foundry: Trap rare — 48.1% GIH and a -4.6 IWD say it plainly: a two-mana rock that makes restricted mana and only pays off with a stocked artifact graveyard. Even the UR artifact deck wants a body or a Sawblades here. Leave it in the sideboard.
Family Reunion: Filler trick at best — 8.3% play rate and a 51.6% that comes almost entirely from the rare committed go-wide GW deck. A one-shot +1/+1 team pump or a fog-on-removal only matters if you have three-plus attackers; a normal deck just wants a body there. Last-pick, sideboard card.
Get Lost: Unconditional two-mana removal that reads better than it plays here: handing an artifact-hungry format two Map tokens (explore fuel, artifact count for UR) is a real cost, and the -2.1 IWD shows it. Still first-pickable interaction, just not a bomb-tier rare.
Glorifier of Suffering: Low-end playable and a WB trap magnet. A 3/2 for three is on-rate, but the sacrifice clause asks you to two-for-one yourself for counters, and -2.2 IWD confirms it's not doing real work. Play it in a committed RW/WU aggro curve, not as a 'sac payoff'.
Guardian of the Great Door: Premium uncommon for any committed white deck — a two-mana 4/4 flier that realistically lands turn four or five once you can tap four permanents. ALSA 3.3 with 87% play rate is correct; it's the flier that breaks the board stalls the doctrine says flying breaks, and it's a top-end payoff in WU/RW.
Helping Hand: Filler that only makes the deck with real ETB creatures to rebuy. Negative IWD at 52.5% means it does nothing on its own — a one-mana sorcery that's blank until something dies. LoL's note describes a bounce spell; ignore it, this is reanimation. 23rd card.
Ironpaw Aspirant: Solid but conditional aggro common — a 1/2 body that only justifies itself when the counter goes on something evasive or a craft/equipment carrier. The -1.1 IWD says it does nothing from the top of the deck; it's a curve card for committed RW/WU aggro, not a card that rescues a half-committed white deck.
Kinjalli's Dawnrunner: High pick for aggressive white — double strike is the one body type where the explore counter is genuinely game-winning (a 2/2 double striker with a pump spell ends games), and 56.7% at 84% play rate confirms it. This is the exception to the explore-on-the-ground trap because the counter scales double.
Kutzil's Flanker: Solid playable, not a rare you commit to. The 3/1 body dies to everything, so most games this is flash-in 'gain 2, scry 2' for three mana or a Hail Mary blocker. 54.2% with a negative IWD means it's replacement-level in a white deck that's already aggressive.
Malamet War Scribe: Solid playable that wants a board, not a curve slot. Five mana for a 4/3 is below rate in a format this cheap, so you're paying for the team pump — it breaks stalls and steals races in go-wide GW/RW. In a half-committed white deck it's near-dead.
Market Gnome: Excellent glue for WU/UR artifacts: a 0/3 wall that stonewalls the format's cheap evasive starts and replaces itself whether it dies or gets eaten by craft. 56.6% GIH on a card that costs one mana and is also craft fodder and Reliquary fuel.
Might of the Ancestors: Marginal, and only in fully committed RW/GW aggro. Repeatable +2/+0 with vigilance is real reach on a wide board, but it does nothing the turn it lands and nothing at all when you're behind — the 35% play rate is the honest verdict on a card that needs the board it can't make.
Miner's Guidewing: Premium one-drop for committed white aggro only. 59.2% with opening-hand WR well above drawn (61.7 vs 57.2) marks it as a turn-one card that goes dead late. LoL's blurb misremembers the text — it's flying vigilance with a dies-trigger explore. Great in RW/WU, near-unplayable in the half-committed white deck.
Mischievous Pup: Solid playable and better than its 52.8% looks — flash 3/1 ambushes two-drops and the optional bounce rebuys any ETB, saves a creature from removal, or resets a craft artifact. The 3/1 body dies to everything, so it's a value two-for-one, not a threat. Mid-pack white pick in any shell.
Ojer Taq, Deepest Foundation: Solid six-drop, not the mythic its stat line implies — this is exactly the big-mana ground body the format punishes. The token-tripling almost never matters in Limited; you are paying six for a 6/6 vigilance that recurs as a land. Take it, don't move in on it.
Oltec Archaeologists: Solid top-end for the craft decks. 27.5% play rate against a 55.0% GIH means it only makes committed WU/artifact decks, where a 4/4 plus scry 3 or artifact rebuy is real value. Playable, but a five-drop you take late, not early.
Oltec Cloud Guard: Best white common in the chunk and a first-pick-quality common overall: four mana for a 3/2 flier plus a Gnome body covers evasion, artifact count, and a blocker in one card. 59.3% GIH with +3.2 IWD across an 89% play rate — take it over almost any ground creature in WU or RW.
Oteclan Landmark: Solid WU craft role-player. One mana to scry 2 is a fine floor, and the flip is a flyer that hands evasion to your ground creature — exactly how this format breaks board stalls. Craft it early, flip when convenient; the 53.3% reflects decks casting it in the wrong shell.
Petrify: Premium cheap white interaction and the reason white's removal suite is the deepest — 2 mana, hits artifacts (Vehicles, crafted equipment) and shuts off activated abilities. LoL's 'poor against big dinosaurs' is overstated: it stops the attack, it just doesn't stop a Staggering Size blowout. Kenji still took Spy Glass Siren over it P1P1; that's how good cheap flyers are, not a knock on this.
Quicksand Whirlpool: Premium white removal, but only in decks that can afford six mana or reliably tap blockers — LoL's control framing is right, and the gap between 54.1% OH and 57.4% GD says it's a card you want to draw later, not lead on. Unconditional exile makes it black's Join the Dead equivalent in white; WU with tappers discounts it constantly.
Resplendent Angel: Bomb — take it and commit to white as LoL says. 61.7% and +7.1 IWD come almost entirely from the front half: a three-mana 3/3 flyer ends board stalls in the format where stalls break on evasion. The Angel token is a bonus you rarely need.
Ruin-Lurker Bat: Premium — one of the best one-drops in the set and an early pick in any white deck. LoL is right that the descend scry is decorative: a turn-one lifelink flyer is the whole card, and the 63.9% opening-hand WR says you want it in the first hand. WU/RW.
Sanguine Evangelist: First-pick bomb — 65.5% GIH and ALSA 1.6 means it never wheels. Three bodies across two triggers, one of them a flyer, and battle cry turns a stalled board into lethal. Fine in any white deck, not just WB; take it over almost anything.
Soaring Sandwing: Solid late-game playable that's never a dead card — plainscycling for {2} means the six-drop turns into a land when you're flooded on plans, not mana. GD WR well above OH WR: this is a stall-breaking flyer, not a curve card, so it fits the medium white deck rather than the hyper-aggressive one.
Spring-Loaded Sawblades: The best cheap interaction in the set and a top-2 white pick. Flash 5 damage kills nearly anything that attacked or got tapped, and the craft into a 5/5 vehicle is pure upside you rarely need. ALSA 2.6 is correct — take it over most rares in WU or RW.
Thousand Moons Crackshot: Only for the fully committed aggro deck (RW/WU). A 2/2 for two is exactly what white wants on the play, but the {2}{W} tap-on-attack is real mana you won't have until turn five. 23.6% play rate says most white decks correctly skip it; the half-committed white deck is where this card is worst.
Thousand Moons Infantry: Sideboard card. A three-mana 2/4 that blocks on both turns is pure defense in a format where white's entire job is attacking — sub-50% GIH and a 15.8% play rate confirm it. Only in a grindy WB/WU shell that needs a wall.
Thousand Moons Smithy: First-pick bomb — the best card in this chunk by a mile. 62.1% GIH, +8.4 IWD and a 1.5 ALSA at 90% play: it makes an immediate must-answer body that scales with your board, and flipping is pure gravy. Take it over anything short of another bomb.
Tinker's Tote: Strong role-player, not filler — two artifact bodies for three mana feeds craft, Captain Storm-style artifact triggers, and go-wide counters in GW, with a lifegain outlet stapled on. Note the tokens do nothing for descend; this is an artifact-count card, not a graveyard card.
Unstable Glyphbridge: Set-defining bomb — first pick, take it over anything. A one-sided wrath that keeps your cheap evasive creatures while sweeping their board, and it later crafts into a flyer that locks the opponent out of attacking. 65% GIH with a 1.6 ALSA; it never wheels.
Vanguard of the Rose: Aggressive two-drop with a real floor — 3 power on turn two matters more here than the sac ability, which taps the creature and mostly just blanks a removal spell. 56.2% on a -0.4 IWD is a pure curve card. Fine in RW/WU; don't draft it expecting a WB sacrifice engine, that pair is the format's trap.
Warden of the Inner Sky: First-pick-quality one-drop — 63.6% GIH and +9.2 IWD off a {W} 1/2 is absurd, and it's earned: WU craft and RW aggro both flood the board with artifacts and creatures, so it turns into a flying vigilant threat that scries every turn. Take it over almost any removal.
Akal Pakal, First Among Equals: Near-bomb engine and a first-pick in UR or WU. The 1/5 stonewalls the aggro decks while every artifact — Map tokens included — buys a filtered card each end step. 62.9% with OH 65.9% above GD: this is a card you want early, not a late-game topdeck.
Ancestral Reminiscence: Filler bordering on sideboard. Four mana, sorcery speed, no board impact — the 11.4% play rate is the real verdict: only a genuine UB or blue control deck with a stabilized board wants it, and even there it's the 23rd card.
Brackish Blunder: Solid tempo playable, not removal — the Map upside makes bouncing a tapped attacker a real two-for-one in WU/UR. Note the weak +0.5 IWD: it does nothing in a vacuum and is dead late. Play it in the tempo decks, cut it from grindy builds.
Braided Net: Strong early pick in WU, not a bomb. Three tapper activations is soft removal with the flexibility to also lock down an opponent's artifact, and it crafts into a real draw engine when the board gums up — exactly the craft-first, flip-when-convenient pattern the format rewards. Combos with any ping or Sawblades.
Chart a Course: Solid playable, not a priority — the -0.3 IWD is the tell that raw card draw doesn't move games in a format this cheap. In WU tempo or UR pirates you attack often enough to draw two clean; in a durdly blue control shell it's a loose two-for-one. Mid-pack pick.
Cogwork Wrestler: Premium blue common and a top-tier WU/UR pick at 57.9% with a 76% play rate. One mana, flash, an artifact for craft and artifact-count payoffs, and the -2/-0 turns a losing block into a free kill or blanks an attacker for a turn. Cheap, evasive-adjacent, always castable — take it early.
Confounding Riddle: Good role-player for blue control and UB descend — the dig mode bins three cards toward descend thresholds while the Force Spike mode punishes a tapped-out curve-out. Drawn WR well ahead of opening-hand WR: it's a mid-game card, not an early one.
Council of Echoes: Strong top-end for UB/BG descend. GD WR (57.3%) far above OH (51.8%) — it's a late-game card, and six mana for a 4/4 flier is fine even when the bounce whiffs. Flying is how board stalls break here, so it closes games the descend shells otherwise can't.
Didact Echo: Filler that only makes UB or BG self-mill decks. Five mana for a 3/2 cantrip is a bad rate on the front, and the descend-4 flying is real but arrives late — the 26% play rate and sub-50% opening-hand number say it's a late-game body you never want early.
Eaten by Piranhas: Good blue interaction but not a kill spell. Flash means you can blow out a combat or shut off an activated ability at instant speed, and it answers bombs cleanly — but the 1/1 body remains, which in a format that wins on chip damage matters. 54.3% with a flat IWD says: playable every blue deck, never a first pick.
The Enigma Jewel: Effectively unplayable in Limited — a 6.6% play rate on a one-mana tapped rock that makes ability-only mana, with a craft cost of {8}{U} plus four activated-ability permanents you'll never assemble. No live WR because nobody ran it; the read is provisional but it points one direction. Take it as a rare and move on.
The Everflowing Well: Strong blue playable on the front half alone — three mana to mill two and draw two is a fine rate, and the flip is a bonus you'll rarely need. Treat this like a craft card: judge the front. The self-mill matters more as descend fuel for UB than as a route to The Myriad Pools.
Frilled Cave-Wurm: Filler at best — 12.2% play rate and 50.3% tell the story. Four mana for a 2/5 that only becomes a 4/5 after you've buried four permanents is a defensive body in a format that rewards cheap evasion. Twenty-third card in a BG or UB descend deck.
Hermitic Nautilus: Solid playable and quietly better than the stat line reads. A two-mana 1/4 vigilance wall that later converts to a 4/1 attacker or a mana-sink removal spell, plus it's an artifact for UR's count. Blocks the format's one- and two-drop aggression on curve.
Hurl into History: Sideboard-to-filler. Five mana held open for a counter is the wrong cost in a format where you must never be the deck with no early plays, and 20.7% play rate says drafters agreed. The discover upside doesn't rescue a reactive five-drop.
Inverted Iceberg: Premium blue common and one of the set's best craft cards. Two mana to replace itself, add to your artifact count for the UR payoffs, and fuel a descend graveyard — all before the flip ever matters. 58.0% GIH with a near-identical OH WR means it's good on every turn of the game.
Kitesail Larcenist: Format bomb, first pick out of any pack. 65.6% GIH and +11.0 IWD: it's a warded 2/3 flyer that also neuters the opponent's best creature permanently while you upgrade your own worst artifact. Blue's flexibility means you can take it blind P1P1.
Lodestone Needle: Premium — 58.3% on an 87% play rate and a +2.1 IWD, the best non-rare blue card in the set. Two stun counters is a three-turn Pacifism on their bomb at flash speed, it's an artifact for craft, and the flipped side grinds explore counters. Doctrine-perfect WU card: judge the front face, flip when convenient.
Malcolm, Alluring Scoundrel: First-pick rare and the format's currency in one card: a two-mana flash flyer that loots every hit. 61.0% GIH with a 64.0% opening-hand WR — it wants to be deployed early and start attacking. Exactly the cheap evasion WU and UR pay for.
Marauding Brinefang: Last-slot filler. Seven mana for a ground 6/7 is exactly the big-mana trap this format punishes — 51.2% GIH with sub-50% opening-hand WR. The real value is islandcycling for {2}: treat it as a land that occasionally becomes a threat, and cut it if your curve is healthy.
Merfolk Cave-Diver: Narrow GU-only build-around and GU is the thinnest pair in the format. A 2/4 blocks well enough to be maindeckable, but you need a real density of explore creatures before the unblockable trigger matters; 36% play rate and 53.1% GIH are the honest ceiling of a niche card.
Oaken Siren: High-priority blue common — take it early in WU and UR. Two-mana flyer with vigilance blocks the aggro starts and still attacks, and it counts as an artifact for Captain Storm/Dowsing Device payoffs. 57.9% with a 58.9% OH WR: it's a curve card, so play it on two.
Ojer Pakpatiq, Deepest Epoch: First-pick bomb. A 4/3 flyer for four in the best colour already beats the format's board stalls, and it returns as a land that re-flips, so removal only buys time. 59.7% with +6.6 IWD and a 1.4 ALSA — it never wheels. Free-roll the double-blue; blue is where you want to be anyway.
Orazca Puzzle-Door: Filler that punches above its play rate — a one-mana artifact that fixes a stumble and feeds descend/artifact counts, with -0.5 IWD confirming it's a smoothing card, not a real card. Playable in UR for the artifact count and UB for the graveyard permanent; cut it from a deck that wants neither.
Out of Air: Sideboard card. Double blue on a counterspell in a format with turn-two pressure means you're holding up four mana you'd rather spend, and the discount only applies to creature spells. 51.9% on a 13.4% play rate — the people playing it are mostly wrong.
Pirate Hat: Archetype-conditional, not a general playable — the -2.9 IWD is the tell. Numot is right that it needs multiple cheap pirates to be worth the equip tax; in UR pirates the rummage smooths every draw, but in anything else it's a card that doesn't affect the board.
Relic's Roar: Trap — negative IWD and a 5% play rate. Turning your own artifact into a 4/3 surprise blocker is cute, but it's a one-mana trick that does nothing on an empty board and blanks against removal. Last card in the pool; don't maindeck it.
River Herald Scout: The set's explore trap in its purest form. A 1/2 body with no evasion means the land half is close to a blank, and the flat IWD confirms drawing it barely helps — Shipwreck Sentry's guaranteed 3/3 is the better card. Playable GU filler, never a reason to move in.
Sage of Days: Archetype-only enabler — 25.9% play rate with a 53.9% WR conditioned on UB/BG descend actually being assembled. A 3/2 body is fine but the mill-three is the point: it's how you hit descend 4 and 8 on schedule. Filler elsewhere, solid in the shell.
Self-Reflection: Late-game value only, not a maindeck default — 51.6% overall but a 48.2% opener versus 53.6% drawn tells you six mana in your opening hand is a liability. Copying a bomb twice across two castings wins long games, so it's a fine 23rd card in a controlling WU/UB deck and a cut in anything aggressive.
Shipwreck Sentry: The fix for explore's ground problem — always a 3/3 for two, and in any deck with Maps, Treasures or a real artifact count it attacks on turn three. Solid common in WU/UR artifact shells; a defensive wall and nothing more elsewhere.
Sinuous Benthisaur: Archetype-conditional payoff. The 54.7% GIH is conditioned on a genuine cave count — at 5-7 Caves this draws two real cards on a 4/4, at two Caves it's a bad six-drop. 35% play rate reflects that. Take it only once your caves are already assembled.
Song of Stupefaction: Sideboard card, and a weak one. It shrinks power only, so the target still blocks and still survives — and it wants the descend count that the doctrine says arrives slowest in the format. 10.9% play rate with flat IWD; only bring it in against a deck built on one big attacker.
Spyglass Siren: Premium uncommon and a genuine P1P1 — Kenji takes it over Petrify and he's right. A one-mana flyer in the best deck (WU, 57.33%) plus a Map token that both fuels artifact payoffs and stores an explore for later. 62.6% GIH with a 65.6% OH WR: it's at its best on turn one.
Staunch Crewmate: Elite two-drop and a genuine P1P1 in blue — 60.4% GIH with the highest opening-hand number in its slot, because a 2/1 on turn two plus a dig for your best artifact/Pirate is exactly the UR and WU game plan. LoL is right that it beats off-colour cards; Kenji taking it over a 6/6 rare is the correct lesson about this format.
Tishana's Tidebinder: Very good blue rare but a skill card — the flash 3/2 body is the floor and always fine, while the ability-strip mode blanks a craft flip, an ETB or an equipment. In a format this artifact-dense it almost always hits something. High pick, just don't hold it waiting for a perfect target.
Unlucky Drop: Playable tempo, not removal — the threat comes back. Four mana instant-speed is fine in WU when you're already ahead on board or need to buy a turn against a bomb you can't kill. 56.7% GIH with a negative IWD: it wins games you were already winning.
Waterlogged Hulk: Trap unless you're the dedicated UB self-mill deck. A one-mana artifact that only taps to mill does nothing for your board, the craft costs four more, and descend 8 is a threshold you hit late or never. Doctrine holds: descend returned the least of any mechanic.
Waterwind Scout: Premium blue common and a core WU piece — exactly the card the format's explore rule likes: variance on a two-power flyer, where the +1/+1 ceiling wins games and the miss still leaves evasion plus a Map. 59.0% GIH at 90% play; take it early.
Waylaying Pirates: Good common for the artifact decks. Four mana for a 3/3 plus a two-turn tempo swing is a genuine attack-enabler in WU/UR, and with the format's artifact density the condition is nearly free. The falling OH-to-GD split says play it as a mid-game push, not a curve filler.
Zoetic Glyph: Near-bomb uncommon in any deck with artifacts to spare — 63.0% with high opening-hand WR means it's a proactive three-drop, not a late add. A 5/4 for two that refunds discover 3 whenever it leaves has no real downside. Count your artifacts first: it's premium in UR and WU, unplayable at four artifacts.
Abyssal Gorestalker: Classic overrated fatty — six mana for a 6/6 with a symmetric double edict, and only 28% of black decks played it. The +3.3 IWD is real (it breaks stalls and eats two blockers' worth of value) but you must be the empty-board control deck for it to be one-sided. One copy as top-end for black control; never a high pick.
Aclazotz, Deepest Betrayal: The best card in the set — 68.4% GIH and +16.8 IWD are format-breaking numbers. A five-mana 4/4 flying lifelink that strips their hand each attack, then returns as a land when killed. P1P1 over anything, splash it off a hidden land if you must.
Another Chance: The engine card of both descend shells. Instant-speed double recursion turns any mill creature into a loop, and a 62% play rate with +3.2 IWD shows it lands. LoL is right that Death-Cap Marionette is the dream partner — but discount it slightly; descend returned less than the guides promised.
Bitter Triumph: Premium removal and a first-pick: unconditional instant-speed kill for two mana with a cost you can nearly always pay. Numot is right that it splashes trivially — hidden lands make it close to free in any deck. +5.2 IWD at ALSA 2.7 is the removal benchmark black otherwise lacks against big threats.
Bloodthorn Flail: Sideboard. 49.0% GIH and a 9.8% play rate — the equip cost is brutal in a format where you'd rather deploy a body, and discarding a card to move it is a real cost black can't pay. Only consider it in a genuinely aggressive shell, which black isn't.
Bringer of the Last Gift: A real bomb but only in BG/UB descend, where the graveyard is stocked and the sweep-plus-reanimate is one-sided. The 56.3% OH against 61.1% GD and +9.4 IWD tells the story: dead in your opener at eight mana, game-ending off the top. Don't take it as a generic fatty, and never cast it before you've filled the yard.
Broodrage Mycoid: Filler at best — 50.7% is near the bottom of playable and a 4/3 for four that needs you to have descended that turn to make a non-blocking token is doing two mediocre jobs. Only the committed BG self-mill build turns it on, and even there it's a 22nd card.
Canonized in Blood: Don't play it. 44.2% is one of the worst numbers in the set, and the reason is the descend trap — this needs real permanent cards hitting your graveyard every turn, which token-makers and chump blocks do not provide. The 4/3 flyer at eight mana is a fantasy.
Chupacabra Echo: Premium removal and a top black pick — take every one, as LoL says. By turn four you usually have two or three permanents in the yard, which kills most of the format's relevant bodies, and the 3/2 attached makes it a genuine two-for-one. The +7.3 IWD is real.
Corpses of the Lost: Strong BG/UB grinder: a 2/2 on arrival that buys itself back every turn you descend, so it converts a long game into an endless token stream. 56.4% GIH is real, but discount it — descend shells underdelivered and this needs self-mill, not tokens, to loop.
Dead Weight: Premium cheap removal and black's best common — take it early. The +3.1 IWD is among the highest in the set because one mana answers the cheap evasive creatures that actually win this format, and it leaves a permanent behind for descend. Just remember black can't kill anything large with it, so pair it with Tithing Blade.
Deathcap Marionette: Good in BG/UB, playable anywhere in black. Deathtouch on a two-drop trades with the RG dinos black otherwise can't answer, and the mill-two is the engine LoL correctly calls the descend archetype's most important card. 55.3% understates it inside the shell.
Deep Goblin Skulltaker: Below replacement at 49.2% — a 2/2 menace for three that only grows if you actually descend, and descend is the mechanic that needed the most work and returned the least. Without self-mill it's a vanilla 2/2 menace three-drop. Playable in a dedicated BG/UB self-mill build, cuttable everywhere else.
Deep-Cavern Bat: Premium two-drop and the backbone of the black control plan, as both guides say — pressure, a lifelink blocker and a stolen removal spell or bomb for two mana. Exiling rather than discarding means killing it gives the card back, so protect it. Take it over most commons and many rares.
Echo of Dusk: Black's best cheap body and a genuine playable outside descend. A 2/2 for two that turns into a 3/3 lifelink once four permanent cards hit the yard — the floor is on-rate, the ceiling stabilizes. 72.7% play rate at 55.2% GIH: auto-include in any black deck.
Fanatical Offering: Good in the shells that generate spare artifacts, mediocre otherwise. With a Map, Treasure, or a dying token it's a two-mana draw two that replaces itself with another Map; with only real creatures to eat it's card-neutral. LoL's BR call is fair, but BR is the format's worst pair — play it in UR/WB artifact and sacrifice builds instead.
Gargantuan Leech: Late-game payoff for a caves build, not a maindeck default. The OH/GD split (49.0% vs 55.5%) is the tell: uncastable early, fine as a topdeck once you have 4+ caves. With five or fewer caves this is an eight-mana 5/5 — cut it. Best in a BG or caves control deck that reaches turn eight.
Grasping Shadows: Skip it — 49.8% and a 46.7% opening-hand number, the worst kind of four-mana enchantment that does nothing the turn it lands and only pays off in a deck attacking alone. Ignore the LoL note, which describes a different card entirely (it is not an instant-speed kill spell). Sideboard-grade at best; the land flip is far too slow.
Greedy Freebooter: Marginal — a 1/1 for one that leaves scry plus a Treasure is fine glue in BR sacrifice or UR artifacts, but 52.0% and 39% play rate say most black decks are control decks that don't want a one-power body. Playable when you have sacrifice outlets, otherwise sideboard.
Join the Dead: Premium removal and the doctrine answer to actual bombs — Dead Weight cannot kill the 4/5 dinos, this can. Take it high but cap at 1-2 copies; triple-costed and dead against the cheap evasive starts. 87.1% play rate and +4.4 IWD confirm it's a maindeck staple.
Malicious Eclipse: Sideboard card. Symmetric -2/-2 is aimed at exactly the cheap evasive creatures that define WU and RW — but a black control deck runs Dead Weight and Tithing Blade and doesn't want to blow up its own blockers. Bring it in against the aggro pairs, not main.
Mephitic Draught: Filler that earns a slot only in UR artifact-count decks, where it's a cheap cantrip that ticks the artifact counter twice. 52.1% GIH and a 33% play rate put it firmly at the back of the deck; never take it over a body or removal.
Preacher of the Schism: Bomb. Deathtouch on a 2/4 blanks the ground while it generates a token or a card every single attack regardless of who's ahead on life, so it's never off. 63.3% GIH with a +11.4 IWD and ALSA 1.6 — first pick, and the reason to be in black.
Primordial Gnawer: Filler that only makes a black deck short on five-drops. A 5/2 trades once, but the discover 3 on death means the body is really a delivery system for a free spell — that's why gd_wr beats oh_wr. 24.6% play rate is about right; last playable.
Queen's Bay Paladin: Overdrafted rare — ALSA 3.2 but only 52.1% GIH, because there are nowhere near enough Vampires to make the recursion trigger. Strip that text and you have a five-mana 5/4 that trades with medium dinos and loses to any removal. Take it as a body if you're already black; don't move in on it.
Rampaging Spiketail: Fine black top-end that is never a dead card — swampcycling for two smooths the early turns, and the ETB indestructible pump turns a block into a two-for-one. Drawn WR far above opening-hand WR: a late-game card, so run one in the BG/UB control build, not two.
Ray of Ruin: Answer-to-anything removal that black badly needs. +4.0 IWD is the highest in this chunk for a common: Dead Weight can't kill the medium dinos, this exiles them plus Vehicles and hidden lands. Five mana sorcery-speed is the cost — play one or two in black control, not three.
Screaming Phantom: Marginal playable. A three-mana 2/2 flier is exactly the kind of cheap evasion the format rewards, but 51.3% GIH says this one underperforms its type line — the body is too small to attack profitably into white and red decks. Fine in UB where the self-mill is live, a late-round pick anywhere else.
Skullcap Snail: Solid black common, mid-pack pick. It trades a card off their hand and leaves a body that blocks a one-drop — the budget Deep Cavern Bat, as LoL says, and it's real hand disruption rather than a descend card. Goes up meaningfully with Another Chance or Defossilize to rebuy the ETB.
Soulcoil Viper: Playable black filler with a reasonable body — the 2/3 blocks the format's two-drops and the reanimation is real value in BG descend or any deck with a genuine best creature. 53.4% and +1.6 IWD is honest mid-pack material, not a card to move in on. Worst in aggro shells where a sorcery-speed sac does nothing.
Stalactite Stalker: Excellent one-drop and a rare that plays like a removal spell — menace plus growth means it threatens damage early and converts into -X/-X on a real threat late, which is exactly what black wants given it can't answer big creatures with Dead Weight. 57.1% with 58.6% OH: play it on turn one. Take it early in any black deck, descend or not.
Starving Revenant: Strong rare, near-first-pickable in black. You're paying four mana for a 4/4 that refuels — the descend 8 drain is irrelevant in most games and shouldn't shape your build. 59.3% and +7.6 IWD; take it in any black deck, control or otherwise.
Stinging Cave Crawler: Solid defensive role-player that trades up all day. A three-mana deathtouch blocker stops the format's dinos cold; the descend-4 draw is a bonus you'll collect maybe twice a game since a 1/3 rarely attacks. Fine in any black deck, never a high pick.
Synapse Necromage: Fine black filler — a 3/1 attacker that leaves two bodies behind, so it trades up and still contributes to sacrifice and descend-adjacent plans. 54.9% GIH is honest mid-deck value; playable in any black deck, exciting in none.
Tarrian's Journal: Playable engine, not an early pick despite the rarity. It converts spare bodies into cards at sorcery speed and eventually recurs creatures, but it affects no board and the sub-52% OH WR shows how badly it clogs an opening hand. Good in BG/BR attrition, a cut in anything that wants to be attacking.
Terror Tide: Archetype-conditional sweeper, not a generic rare. gd_wr 4pp above oh_wr confirms it's a late-game card and the X only counts permanent CARDS in your graveyard — tokens and instants do nothing. In a real BG/UB descend deck it's a one-sided wrath; in any other black deck it's a bad Shrivel.
Tithing Blade: Premium black common — 56.8% and a +4.6 IWD off two mana. LoL has it exactly right: the edict is the card, the flip is fantasy, and you get an artifact rectangle for descend and craft on top. Answers hexproof and go-tall threats Dead Weight can't. Take roughly two per black deck.
Visage of Dread: Solid two-mana disruption for UR artifacts and black descend — a targeted Thoughtseize on their best creature or artifact, plus permanent artifact count from turn two. Craft it only when you have nothing better to do with six mana; judge it on the front face, which is already playable.
Vito's Inquisitor: Sideboard. 48.5% GIH and a 24.8% play rate are damning: a vanilla 3/3 for four whose ability eats your own permanents for menace counters. The WB sacrifice deck it wants is the format's trap pair. Don't play it.
Abrade: Premium red removal, take it over almost any creature. Three damage at instant speed kills the format's key cheap evasive threats, and the artifact mode is genuinely live in a set this artifact-dense — it answers Diamond Pick-Axe, crafted equipment, and Captain Storm's support. ALSA 2.7, 91% play rate; it goes as early as red does.
Ancestors' Aid: Good trick only in a fully committed aggro deck — RG or RW. +2/+0 and first strike wins basically any combat this format offers, and the Treasure ramps you into the next dino or fixes a splash. The 44.8% play rate against a 55.8% GIH is the warning: right deck only, and the wrong deck should not play it.
Belligerent Yearling: Excellent RG two-drop — 3/2 trample on turn two already pressures, and in a real dino deck it becomes the biggest thing on board for free. The 59.2% OH versus 55.8% GD is the signature of a curve card: great early, mediocre topdeck. High pick in Gruul, which the data ranks 3rd despite LoL's B+.
Bonehoard Dracosaur: The best card in the set — 70.1% GIH and +17.0 IWD off a five-mana 5/5 flying first striker that wins the game on its own the turn after it lands. P1P1 over anything, splash for it off hidden lands. Kill it on sight from the other side.
Brass's Tunnel-Grinder: Mediocre rare that reads better than it plays. The ETB is a rummage, the flip needs three separate descend turns, and the artifact itself does nothing to the board. 53.8% with OH above GD is a fine three-drop artifact for UR's artifact count — never a build-around.
Brazen Blademaster: Filler, and only in UR. The -3.7 IWD is the worst in this group — off the artifact condition it's a three-mana 2/3 with no evasion, which the format lapped. Playable when you already have nine artifacts, cuttable the moment you have a real three-drop.
Breeches, Eager Pillager: First-pick rare. A three-mana 3/3 first striker is already above rate in this format, and the attack trigger is unconditional card advantage or an unblockable alpha strike. 64.8% GIH at ALSA 1.4 — it never wheels, and you don't need a pirate deck.
Burning Sun Cavalry: Fine aggressive two-drop in RG/RW with a real dinosaur count. OH WR three points above GD WR marks it as a pure curve card — it wants to be cast on turn two and attack, and it fades hard in the late game. Playable filler, easily replaced by anything with evasion.
Calamitous Cave-In: Build-around, never a P1P1 — 48.5% opening-hand versus 55.6% drawn is the signature of a card that needs the deck already built. With 5-7 caves plus a Compass Gnome it's a repeatable Pyroclasm that the tempo decks cannot play through. Wheel it at pick 6-9 and commit.
Child of the Volcano: Cut it — 47.6% is one of the worst numbers in red, and a 13.5% play rate confirms it. A 3/3 trample for four is already below rate in a format where flyers and equipment break stalls, and red rarely descends reliably enough to grow it. Sideboard even in BR.
Curator of Sun's Creation: Filler outside a dedicated discover build. A four-mana 3/3 with no immediate impact is a bad rate in this format, and the 51.6% GIH at only 33.7% play rate says the doubler rarely triggers. Needs several discover cards to justify the slot.
Daring Discovery: Niche finisher, not a maindeck card — 11.8% play rate says most red decks correctly cut it. Five mana to alpha-strike through blockers plus a free four-drop wins a stalled board, but it does nothing when you're behind. 24th card that gets sideboarded in.
Diamond Pick-Axe: High pick in any aggressive deck: one mana, indestructible so removal can't two-for-one you, and each attack ramps and fixes. The OH/GD split (58.7 vs 54.8) is the tell — it's a card you want on turn one alongside a creature, not a topdeck. Best in RW and UR where it also pads artifact count.
Dinotomaton: Strong red common, take it around pick 4-6. A four-mana 4/3 menace is above rate in this format and menace is a genuine evasion mode when boards clog; it also counts as an artifact for UR. Flat IWD and a 55.4% GIH = reliable beater, not a game-breaker.
Dire Flail: Strong RW/UR pick and one of the cheapest ways to break a board stall — one mana, equip 1, so it comes down turn one and keeps attacking through the mid-game. 58.3% at a 2.1 ALSA, and the craft gives you a late-game machine gun without ever needing a spare artifact early. Judge the front face; the flip is gravy.
Dowsing Device: Archetype-conditional and the numbers are honest about it: 52.8% with -2.5 IWD means it's a dead card outside UR. LoL calls it engine-core, and it is — but the engine needs 9+ artifacts and map tokens. Late pick that becomes a solid playable only once you're committed to Izzet artifacts.
Dreadmaw's Ire: The best kind of trick in this format — one mana, +2/+2 and trample turns a dino into a blowout, and the artifact-destruction rider punishes the equipment and Map decks. 57.7% at 83.1% play; take it mid-pack for RG or RW and play every copy.
Enterprising Scallywag: Fine aggressive two-drop — grade the body, not the rider. Without self-mill you'll descend on maybe half your turns, so treat the Treasure as occasional fixing rather than a plan. A 2/2 for two that curves is what earns its slot in RG/RW/UR.
Etali's Favor: Strong red common because the discover 3 pays for the aura before the two-for-one risk matters — you get a card, then trample on top. 57.6% GIH in RG/RW beatdown. Put it on something already evasive or hard to kill, not a fresh one-drop.
Geological Appraiser: Near-premium uncommon — take it over most on-plan cards. LoL's 'Chupacabra tier' call holds up: four mana for a 3/2 plus a free three-drop is two-for-one tempo, and 59.8% GIH on an 89% play rate proves it isn't build-dependent. Keep the curve low so discover doesn't whiff.
Goblin Tomb Raider: Aggro one-drop, priority in UR artifacts and RW. The +0.2 IWD next to a 57.1% GIH is the artifact condition talking: a hasty 2/2 on turn one when you're on plan, a 1/2 that does nothing when you aren't. Take it only after your artifact count is real.
Goldfury Strider: Defensive role-player at 53.2% — a 3/5 trample body that walls dinos and counts as an artifact for UR, and the tap-two pump lets you push the last few points through a stall. Five mana with no immediate impact means it's a 21st-22nd card, not a pick you make over cheap interaction.
Hit the Mother Lode: Unplayable at seven mana — 4.6% play rate and a sub-50% win rate even among the few decks that tried it. Discover 10 off a Limited pool hits a four-drop and some Treasures. Sideboard it.
Hotfoot Gnome: Filler that only earns its slot on artifact count. A 3/1 haste for three is fragile in a format full of cheap interaction (-2.3 IWD), but it's a body that counts for UR's 9+ artifact plan and Captain Storm triggers. Playable in UR, cuttable everywhere else.
Idol of the Deep King: Solid playable, and LoL's blurb describes a different card — this is a flash artifact that Shocks any target, then crafts into a +2/+0 equipment later. Read it as a two-for-one on the front face: instant-speed reach or a small kill, plus artifact count and craft fodder. The negative IWD reflects that it's curve filler, not a bomb.
Inti, Seneschal of the Sun: First-pick-quality rare — 62.0% GIH, 1.5 ALSA. A two-drop that turns every attack into a pump plus card advantage, and the discard is upside not cost since you get to play the exiled card. The 64.9% OH WR says get it down early; it's an aggro engine, so pair it with RW or RG.
Magmatic Galleon: The best card in this chunk and a slam first pick — 65.5% GIH with +11.0 IWD, because five damage on entry kills basically anything and leaves a 5/5 artifact that crews off a single two-power body. It's removal, a threat and an artifact count in one card. Nothing in UR or RG comes close.
Ojer Axonil, Deepest Might: Strong red four-drop — a 4/4 trampler that recurs as a land is a fine body plus insurance, and the damage-amplification clause turns any burn spell into a 4-point hit in a deck with Cosmic Blast and pingers. 57.6% is good but not bomb territory; take it over solid removal only in a committed red deck.
Panicked Altisaur: Solid common top-end, and correct the note — it's five mana, not seven. A 4/5 reach body walls flyers while the tap ability provides inevitability against control mirrors. 56.2% and 67.4% play means one is right for a grindy RG deck, two is one too many.
Plundering Pirate: Strong red common and a high pick for UR. Three mana for 3/2 plus an artifact is exactly the two-for-one the Izzet count wants, and the Treasure also fixes the near-free splashes that hidden lands enable. Take it over most red three-drops.
Poetic Ingenuity: Archetype-conditional build-around, not a slam. The 62.7% opening-hand vs 54.8% drawn split says it must land early to pay off, and it needs both dinos attacking and artifacts to cast. Great in a committed RG/UR shell; a mediocre three-drop anywhere else.
Rampaging Ceratops: Solid RG top end that genuinely breaks stalls — needing three blockers is functional evasion, not a stat line, which spares it the big-dumb-fatty trap. Still a five-drop with no immediate impact, so it's a finisher you play one or two of, not a card you take over cheap interaction.
Rumbling Rockslide: Playable removal, low priority. Four mana sorcery-speed is a full turn behind Cosmic Blast in a format that punishes durdling, and the -1.5 IWD reflects it. Kills essentially anything once you're on four-plus lands, so it makes the deck as red's fifth-best removal spell — not a pick you steer on.
Saheeli's Lattice: Strong two-drop for UR artifacts — 56.0% with identical opening and drawn win rates, so it's never a dead card. Rummage-into-two is real card advantage at two mana, it feeds artifact count and craft fodder, and the Raptor flip is pure upside you take only if you're deep in dinos. Early-mid pick in red.
Scytheclaw Raptor: High-priority aggressive uncommon: a three-mana 4/3 is above-rate on its own and outclasses most of the format's three- and four-drops in combat. The punisher clause is a tax that freezes their tricks, not a win condition. Core RG/RW playable, 89.3% play rate for a reason.
Seismic Monstrosaur: Playable top-end with a real floor. Six mana for a 6/5 trample is the stat line the doctrine warns about, but mountaincycling for {2} means it's never a dead card, which is why it's played 60% of the time at only 53.2%. One copy max in RG/RW.
Sunfire Torch: Fine early-pick artifact for the aggro decks. One mana of +1/+0 that converts into two damage on your terms functions as removal on a delay, and it's an artifact for craft and UR payoffs. Negative IWD confirms the pattern: play it on turn one, don't be happy to draw it on turn eight.
Sunshot Militia: Underrated red common. The 1/3 body blocks the format's aggressive two-drops profitably, and the tap ability turns spare Maps, Treasures and vigilance creatures into a real clock once the ground stalls. 56.0% GIH; best in UR artifacts where you have bodies to spare.
Tectonic Hazard: Sideboard only — 1 damage to their board is a blank against almost every relevant creature in a format this full of 2/3s and 3/3s. 46.7% on a 1.7% play rate says the drafters who ran it were desperate. Bring it in against go-wide GW counters decks or Gnome tokens, otherwise leave it in the pile.
Triumphant Chomp: Premium-adjacent red removal in RG, ordinary elsewhere. One mana for 2 damage is playable filler; one mana for 5-6 in a dino deck is one of the best interaction rates in the set. 56.9% at 83% play rate reflects the blended reality — take it high if you're green-red, mid-pack otherwise.
Trumpeting Carnosaur: Format-defining bomb and the easiest P1P1 in the set. 63.5% with +9.4 IWD because it's never a dead card: either a 7/6 trample that discovers into a free spell, or a three-damage removal spell for three mana when you're flooded or off-curve.
Volatile Wanderglyph: Excellent cheap red common — a two-mana 2/2 artifact body that also fixes your draws every time it attacks or crews. The 59% opening-hand WR marks it as a curve card you want early. Core UR playable; still fine as a generic red two-drop.
Zoyowa's Justice: Do not play this. 43.8% GIH and -6.6 IWD — one of the worst cards in the set. You spend two mana, don't permanently answer anything, and hand the opponent a free discover. A 4.7% play rate is the correct number.
Armored Kincaller: One of green's best commons and a fine RG playable. A three-mana 3/3 already meets the format's rate, and the three life is a real buffer against the aggressive decks — 56.7% GIH with identical OH and GD WRs means it's good whenever you draw it. Take it over any explore body.
Basking Capybara: Near-unplayable outside a fully-built descend deck. A 1/3 for two blocks early and a 4/3 with no evasion or reach does nothing to break the flyer-and-equipment stalls this format ends on. 50.9% at 30.6% play rate — the hosts were right that it's bad at both ends.
Bedrock Tortoise: Green's best rare here at 60.8% and ALSA 1.8 — it attacks as a 6/6 and blocks as a 0/6 that nothing profitably runs into, and the on-your-turn team hexproof blanks their removal during combat. It turns every green toughness-heavy body into a real threat. First-pickable; commit to green when you see it.
Cavern Stomper: The green common you actually want as top-end — scry 2 smooths the miss and the evasion activation breaks the stall it creates. Strong at 56.9%, but it's still six mana in a cheap format: play one, two only with real ramp or 18 lands.
Cenote Scout: Premium green one-drop and the exception to the explore-on-the-ground rule — at one mana the coin flip is free either way. 61.1% opening-hand WR against 55.9% drawn: this is a card you want in your opener, so take it early and play it on turn one.
Coati Scavenger: Archetype-conditional — a fine 3/2 body that turns into a two-for-one only in a real BG self-mill deck. The 6pp gap between opening-hand (50.2%) and drawn (56.0%) is the whole story: it's a mid-to-late card you want after your graveyard is stocked. Just a bear in a generic green deck.
Colossadactyl: Top green uncommon — a 3.1 ALSA means you take it early. Reach plus trample on a 4/5 for four dominates the ground and shuts off the flyers that otherwise break stalls, which is the specific hole green decks have. 57.2% across the board with no OH/GD split: just a great card any time you draw it.
Disturbed Slumber: Last-card filler. A 4/4 must-be-blocked land is a combat trick that costs you a land drop's worth of vulnerability, and at 48.0% with a 3.2% play rate the format has voted. It can steal a game as a surprise blocker-eater or an unexpected reach blocker, but never maindeck it over a real playable.
Earthshaker Dreadmaw: Genuine bomb for RG despite the doctrine's warning about six-mana ground fatties — the ETB draws real cards, so it isn't a do-nothing body. LoL's "incredible magic card" holds up at 57.0%. Worth noting the card draw is conditional on your board already existing; it's a payoff, not a stabilizer.
Explorer's Cache: Fine role-player in GW counters, filler elsewhere. Two mana that slowly buys +1/+1 counters and recycles them off dying creatures — it never affects the board the turn you cast it. 55.4% with OH above GD: play it early in the curve or not at all.
Ghalta, Stampede Tyrant: The doctrine's biggest-mana trap in card form. Eight mana for a ground creature in a format decided by two-drop flyers and craft — the 59.8% play rate says four in ten drafters who opened it left it in the sideboard. Only playable in a real green ramp deck with creatures to dump.
Glimpse the Core: Near-trap. A two-mana ramp spell that adds no board presence is exactly what you can't afford here, and the Cave recursion mode is dead in most decks. Negative IWD at 36% play. Only consider it in a heavy-cave green control build.
Glowcap Lantern: Don't play it. Explore attached to Equipment stacks two of the format's weaknesses — the equip tax costs you a turn and the payoff is ground-creature explore, the exact effect the data hates. 48.7% GIH and a 30% play rate; it's sideboard material even in GU.
Growing Rites of Itlimoc: Rare trap at 50.3%. Three mana for a creature tutor that affects no board is exactly the durdle this format kills, and the flip needs four creatures already down — by which point you'd rather have drawn a dinosaur. Green's mana is not the constraint. Cut it.
Huatli, Poet of Unity: Bomb — 65.7% GIH and a +12.9 IWD, top of the set. A two-mana body that fixes, then flips for six 3/3s worth of board across the Saga plus a double-strike alpha strike. Even without the {R/W} flip mana she's a fine ramping two-drop. P1P1, and it's the reason to be in RG/Naya dinos.
Huatli's Final Strike: Green's premium removal and a top-tier common — instant-speed, no damage back, and a three-mana answer to nearly anything once you're the RG deck with a 4-power dino. 57.4% at an 84.4% play rate. Requires a board, so don't stack too many.
Hulking Raptor: Near-bomb rare and a hard signal to be green. Unlike the big dinos that punish you, this is cheap: a 5/3 ward 2 on four that immediately ramps you to a six-drop on five. 59.1% GIH with a 1.7 ALSA — it goes in every green deck and it's the reason RG finished 3rd, not the B+ LoL gave the pair.
In the Presence of Ages: Build-around only, and Numot is right that it beats Another Chance in the turbo-Bringer BG shell because it finds a land too. 15.9% play rate means almost nobody's deck wanted it — take it late, and only when you have self-mill payoffs. The instant speed is a real perk on a dig-plus-mill spell.
Intrepid Paleontologist: Take it high in green — 61.1% GIH, 1.8 ALSA. A two-mana body that fixes and ramps is already fine on rate, and the dino recursion converts a long game into inevitability in RG or Jund. The 62.8% OH WR means the mana ability is doing the work; you don't need the dino package for it to be good.
Ixalli's Lorekeeper: Narrow — a one-mana 1/1 whose mana only casts Dinosaurs, so it's only playable in a genuinely dino-dense RG build. The 60.0% OH against 52.4% GD is the clearest tell in the chunk: it ramps from your opener and is a dead draw after turn four. Playable in Gruul, unplayable elsewhere.
Jade Seedstones: Solid playable in GW counters and green aggro — three counters spread across a wide board is a two-for-one in combat and the craft flip is pure upside you'll rarely reach. 54.2% OH vs 57.3% GD says it's a mid-game card, so don't play it in a deck without bodies to put counters on.
Jadelight Spelunker: Strong rare and the one explore card that beats the on-the-ground trap, because you choose X — cast it for four or five and the misses no longer matter. 59.0% with +5.6 IWD; it's both a curve-filler and a late-game mana sink in any green deck.
Kaslem's Stonetree: Unplayable outside a fringe caves build. Three mana to find one land while your opponent deploys a body is exactly what you can't afford, and the craft costs six. The 47.7% is the floor of this group — cut it.
Malamet Battle Glyph: Green's best interaction and a high pick in RG/GW — one mana to fight is a real removal rate, and the +1/+1 counter off a fresh ETB means you win fights you shouldn't. 57.4% GIH. Only caveat: it's blank when you're behind on board.
Malamet Brawler: Filler at best. LoL is right that it's a card missing its support — trample on an attacker matters only once you have a big creature, and a 2/2 for two without a Dinosaur type does nothing for RG's payoffs. 52.1% GIH at 7.7 ALSA: late-pick, 23rd-card territory.
Malamet Scythe: Serviceable equipment, late pick. Flash-and-attach means a surprise +2/+2 blowout the first time, and equipment is one of the legitimate stall-breakers here, but Equip 4 is prohibitive after the body dies. ALSA 8.1 and 20.3% play rate — take it as a 22nd card in a creature-dense green deck.
Malamet Veteran: Top-end common for RG/BG — 52.5% with a 27% play rate says it's the 22nd card in a green deck, not a priority. A 5/4 trample for five does close games against ground stalls, but the descend 4 rider is inert in most builds. Fine to take late; never over a cheap evasive body.
Mineshaft Spider: Role-player, not a body you want on rate. The 3/4 reach blanks the WU and UR flyers that actually win this format, and the mill two is a genuine descend enabler for BG/UB — the doctrine build-around list names it. Sideboard-in against blue, maindeck in descend.
Nurturing Bristleback: Good ceiling-setter for RG/GW. Eight power across two bodies ends the games where dino decks grind; forestcycling makes the clunk survivable, which is why it's played 70% of the time at 55.1%. One is right, two makes your curve top-heavy in a format this cheap.
Ojer Kaslem, Deepest Growth: First-pick bomb, the highest-impact card in this chunk. A five-mana 6/5 trampler that snowballs permanents off any connection and comes back as a land that re-transforms — it wins the game alone if it attacks twice. 64.4% GIH and +12.0 IWD at ALSA 1.3; never pass it.
Over the Edge: Marginal maindeck, 23rd-card territory at 51.8%. The explore mode falls into the set's biggest trap — double explore on a ground creature is a coin flip that often hands you two lands and a whiff. Keep one in the board: artifacts are everywhere here, and killing an Equipment or a craft card is where this earns its slot.
Pathfinding Axejaw: One of green's best commons — a 4/3 for four that explores, which here means it's usually a 5/4 and never a total whiff. Correct the LoL note: this is a common, not the RG signpost rare. It's also the counterexample to the explore trap, because the body is already above rate before the counter. Solid mid pick in any green deck.
Poison Dart Frog: Better than it looks — reach blocks the flyers that break stalls, the mana lets green midrange jump to turn-three four-drops, and deathtouch activation makes it an attack deterrent all game. 60.3% opening-hand WR is the tell: this is a turn-two play, not a topdeck. Resolve LoL's debate toward midrange, not dino aggro.
Pugnacious Hammerskull: Top-tier rare — 64.0% GIH, 66.4% opening hand and +10.0 IWD, among the best in the set. A 6/6 for three outclasses everything on the ground, and the stun counter stops mattering the moment you have a second Dinosaur. RG's best non-mythic beater.
River Herald Guide: Mediocre, and the exemplar of the explore trap. When it misses you have a 3/1 vigilance that dies to everything and trades with nothing; you want the counter, not the land. Shipwreck Sentry, an unconditional 3/3, is the better card at the same slot. Late GU/RG filler.
Seeker of Sunlight: Filler at best. This is the doctrine's ground-explore problem in its purest form: a 1/1 body paying three mana per activation to maybe grow, on a creature with no evasion. 51.5% GIH and 27% play — take a real two-drop instead.
Sentinel of the Nameless City: Best card in this batch and a first-pick rare. A vigilant 3/4 for three already blanks the format's aggressive starts, and the Map-per-attack stream turns every turn into a stored explore plus an artifact for the artifact payoffs. 64.6% GIH with +11.1 IWD — take it and play green.
The Skullspore Nexus: Bomb, and cheaper than it reads — with a 4-power dino out it's a four-mana mythic that turns every creature death into a huge token and doubles power to close. 60.9% GIH with 83.1% play rate across green decks. Take it over any common and let the eight-mana printed cost scare someone else.
Spelunking: Build-around that didn't pay off — 50.7% on a 13% play rate. The ETB replaces itself and the untapped-lands clause matters only if you're running 5-7 caves plus hidden lands, and even then you'd rather have a creature. Playable in a dedicated caves/control deck; a cut in every other green deck.
Staggering Size: Best combat trick in the set, and LoL admitted undervaluing it — two mana, +3/+3 and trample turns any RG dino into lethal through a chump block. It still wheels at 7.3 ALSA, so take the creature first and pick this up on the back half.
Tendril of the Mycotyrant: Solid green two-drop with a late-game mana sink built in. Even OH/GD splits (55.5%/56.8%) mean it's fine at both ends of the game — an on-curve body early, a 7/7 haste land when you flood. 78.6% play at 4.4 ALSA: a quiet, always-playable green card.
Thrashing Brontodon: Premium green uncommon and one of the best rate creatures in the set. A 3/4 for three blanks the format's aggressive two- and three-drops, and the sacrifice ability is rarely dead when artifacts and equipment are everywhere. Take it early in RG or GW; 57.5% GIH with an 87% play rate is honest, no synergy required.
Twists and Turns: GU-only build-around with a real payoff but a narrow home. Scry-before-explore fixes the exact problem explore has — you stop missing — but you need a critical mass of explore creatures to justify a one-mana do-nothing. The gd/oh split (57.1% vs 53.0%) says it's a mid-game engine; GU is thin at 3.9% share, so only when it's open.
Walk with the Ancestors: Marginal at five mana — you get a card back plus a discover 4 hit, which is real raw value, but 52.9% and a 22.4% play rate means it's too slow for most decks. Only worth it in a BG/GU grind build with a strong permanent in the yard and a curve tight enough not to whiff. 23rd card otherwise.
Abuelo, Ancestral Echo: High pick in WU — a warded 2/2 flyer for three is already on-plan for the best deck in the format, and the blink ability rebuys ETBs, saves a creature from removal, or resets a craft artifact. 58.4% with +4.4 IWD. Take it over most gold cards; it needs no build-around.
Akawalli, the Seething Tower: Good BG payoff with a real floor — a 3/3 for three that grows to a 5/5 trampler is fine even on a half-built descend deck. 55.3% at 58.9% play is archetype-conditional; feed it with self-mill like Death-Cap Marionette, never with token generation.
Amalia Benavides Aguirre: Trap rare in the trap pair. Ward-3-life on a two-mana 2/2 is a fine aggressive body, but the power-20 payoff never assembles in Limited and WB is the format's worst-built pair. The 38.5% play rate says most drafters correctly left it out of the deck.
The Ancient One: Powerful but conditional — descend 8 means it's a looting mana sink for many turns before it's an 8/8, and only a dedicated UB self-mill shell turns it on. The 57.5% GIH and +8.3 IWD are conditioned on that deck existing; 60% play rate says it often didn't.
Anim Pakal, Thousandth Moon: Bomb in committed RW aggro, near-blank anywhere else. The token generation compounds brutally but only if you attack every turn, which is why the 66% OH WR outruns its drawn WR — it wants to be cast on turn three into an existing board. Take it high, then actually build the aggressive deck.
Bartolomé del Presidio: The signpost for the format's worst-real pair, and 52.0% says so. A 2/1 for two that grows only by eating your own board is fine in an aggressive white curve but WB is the trap — mediocre aggro stapled to mediocre descend. Play it if you're already there; don't let it pull you in.
The Belligerent: Strong UR rare at 56.2%, but crew 3 is the real cost — you need two bodies or one big one to attack with it, and it does nothing on an empty board. When it does connect the Treasure plus top-of-library access snowballs a game in two swings. Early pick in UR artifacts, worse in any deck with few creatures.
Caparocti Sunborn: Strong RW signpost: a four-mana 4/4 beats the format's common four-drops straight up, and the discover 3 is free value whenever you have a spare Map or an untapped body. Tapping two attackers is a real cost in a race, so trigger it on the turns you're not all-in.
Captain Storm, Cosmium Raider: Premium UR signpost — take it early and kill it on sight. 62.7% opening-hand WR (well above its 57.2% drawn) says it's a turn-two play that snowballs, exactly LoL's 'gets out of hand fast'. The flip side: hold cheap instant-speed removal for it or you lose quickly.
Deepfathom Echo: Strong rare, and LoL's blurb misremembers it — it's a 4/4 ground body for four that explores every combat and can copy your best creature. The +8.5 IWD is real; it grows itself and doesn't need a built explore deck to be excellent. High pick in GU, worth a splash off hidden lands elsewhere.
Gishath, Sun's Avatar: Trap, and the data is blunt about it — 51.3% GIH and a 49.0% OH WR on a mythic. Eight mana across three colors in a format that punishes having no early plays, and it does nothing the turn it lands unless you're already winning. Hidden lands make the splash castable; they don't make it worth the pick.
Itzquinth, Firstborn of Gishath: Premium Gruul uncommon — a hasty 2/3 for two that also fires a removal spell when you have any dinosaur online, all for {2}. 61.2% GIH and +4.7 IWD make it one of the best two-drops in the format if you're RG. Take it over most commons; the signpost is doing real work here, unlike most gold uncommons.
Kellan, Daring Traveler: Excellent white two-drop and one of the format's best curve-fillers — a 2/3 body blocks everything early, and the attack trigger refuels the low-curve white deck that otherwise runs out of gas. 62.3% OH WR says play it on turn two. The Map-token back half is a fine mode when you're flooded.
Kutzil, Malamet Exemplar: Quietly excellent in GW, the 5th-best and most underdrafted pair. A 3/3 for three that draws cards off any pumped or countered creature, and the no-instants clause makes your attacks math-free. 56.7% with 55.1% play — it's better than the field treats it.
Master's Guide-Mural: Premium payoff for WU and a strong pick once you're in the colors — a 4/4 on arrival with a token factory attached is how the best deck closes a board stall. Heed LoL: the {4}{W}{W}{U} craft means don't splash this from UB, you'll never cast the flip.
Molten Collapse: Premium removal stapled to the format's worst colour pair. Two mana for unconditional creature kill is worth building toward, and the 58.5% drawn vs 53.0% opening-hand gap just means you want descend online to double up. Take it, but don't let it drag you into BR.
The Mycotyrant: Build-around that underdelivered. A 50.0% OH WR on a three-mana mythic is damning: it's a 0/0 on an empty board and its own tokens only grow it, not your descend count. BG can make it work with self-mill, but don't take it over a clean removal spell or a real body.
Nicanzil, Current Conductor: Narrow GU uncommon at 52.7%. A 2/3 for two is a real body, but the payoff is explore triggers and GU is a 3.9%-share pair whose explore creatures are the format's ground-creature trap. Playable filler in Simic, not a reason to be Simic.
Palani's Hatcher: P1P1 bomb — 67.5% and a +13.6 IWD, one of the highest numbers in the set. Five power of haste on turn five plus a 3/3 every combat forever means one untapped turn wins; giving your other dinos haste stacks the alpha strike. LoL is right to draft Jund around it: commit the moment you see it.
Quintorius Kand: Bomb. 62.7% GIH and +10.1 IWD — the +1 makes a 3/2 every turn, which alone wins an unanswered board, and -3 discover 4 refuels. Five mana and gold, but RW is a top-four pair; take it and commit.
Saheeli, the Sun's Brilliance: Good, not a bomb — the mythic rarity oversells it. +0.1 IWD and 54.6% GIH: a 2/2 for two that needs surviving plus a worthwhile copy target before it does anything. Excellent alongside ETB creatures in UR artifacts, mediocre in a generic pile.
Sovereign Okinec Ahau: Good in GW, unexciting anywhere else — a 3/4 with ward 2 is hard to remove but the counters only stack when your other creatures are already bigger than their printed base power, which needs a go-wide pump board. 54.5% GIH on a mythic is a soft number; the OH/GD split says play it on curve, not as a late-game haymaker.
Squirming Emergence: Descend payoff that underdelivered — 49.7% GIH and a 45.3% OH WR, which is dire for a three-mana rare. It needs four-plus permanent CARDS in the yard (tokens don't count) before it returns anything meaningful, and BG at 54.42% isn't the shell to bend a deck around. Playable in a self-mill build with Another Chance and Death-Cap Marionette; otherwise cut.
Uchbenbak, the Great Mistake: A fine five-drop body that most decks shouldn't be reaching for — 6/4 vigilance menace pressures and blocks well, but the descend 8 recursion needs a dedicated UB self-mill shell, and UB underdelivered at 53.66%. 54.0% with a 52.4% play rate says it's a UB-only card. Don't splash for it; the front half alone isn't worth the gold cost.
Vito, Fanatic of Aclazotz: Bomb-level stats (+10.0 IWD) attached to the format's trap pair — a 4/4 flyer for four wins games on rate alone, so take it, but do not let it drag you into WB sacrifice, which finished 9th at 52.87%. Treat it as a mono-black-splash-white flyer and the sacrifice text as occasional upside.
Wail of the Forgotten: Archetype-conditional and worth discounting. OH 51.8% against GD 58.9% marks it as a late card you need descend 8 online to make good, and UB was the shell that most underdelivered. Two mana for one weak mode early is a real cost — a mid-pack pick in UB only.
Zoyowa Lava-Tongue: Grindy role-player, not an aggro two-drop — LoL's framing is correct. Deathtouch makes it a fine early blocker, and the end-step trigger drains a stalled opponent's hand and board. But it lives in BR, the format's worst pair, so it's rarely worth moving into.
Buried Treasure: Cut it. 48.8% GIH and -2.6 IWD — a ramp/fixing rock that does nothing for the board, and the five-mana graveyard discover is a late-game luxury you rarely reach profitably. Only a splash-fixing consideration, and Caves do that job better.
Careening Mine Cart: Playable artifact-count filler for UR. Crew 1 is trivially easy and a 3/3 attacker that makes Treasure is fine pressure plus fixing, but the OH-above-GD split flags it as an early-game card that gets outclassed fast. Take it for the artifact triggers more than the body.
Cartographer's Companion: Filler with a job. A 3-mana 2/1 is below rate — the -2.2 IWD is honest — but it's two artifact bodies for Captain Storm, Dowsing Device and Zoetic Glyph triggers plus a stored explore. Take it as a playable in UR artifacts, cut it everywhere else.
Compass Gnome: Role-player, not the all-star LoL calls it — 52.2% with a negative IWD is the data's verdict on a 2/1 that fetches a land. What it actually buys you is cheap splashes off hidden lands, cave count, and an artifact for craft/descend. Take it mid-to-late when your deck needs the fixing, not as a pick-two.
Contested Game Ball: Unplayable — 0.8% play rate and no meaningful win-rate sample. It gives itself to whoever attacks you, and the draw engine costs two per card in a format that doesn't grind that long. Provisional read from the text, but the direction is not close.
Digsite Conservator: Colorless filler that fits any deck's artifact count. A 2/1 for two is on-rate in a fast format, and paying {4} on death for discover 4 turns a bad trade into a real card. 53.5% GIH at 69% play — a fine 21st-23rd card, never a pick you make early.
Disruptor Wanderglyph: Cut it. Four mana for a colorless 3/4 with an irrelevant attack trigger is exactly the medium ground body this format punishes, and 48.1% GIH with -3.0 IWD and a 4.8% play rate is the format agreeing. Graveyard hate is not worth a maindeck slot even against descend decks.
Hoverstone Pilgrim: Defensive top-end for the slower blue decks. A 2/5 flyer with ward 2 is nearly impossible to remove and stonewalls the evasive creatures that actually win this format, plus it grinds opposing graveyards. But five mana for a body that doesn't attack well is why it sits at 53.6% with a 50.7% OH WR — a fine 20th card in UB, not a pick you reach for.
Hunter's Blowgun: Sideboard-adjacent filler — equip 2 is too expensive for a format where the tempo decks are already attacking, and 50.1% with a -2.6 IWD confirms it. The offense/defense mode-switch is cute and the deathtouch does break a ground stall, but a 9.0% play rate means you should be finding a real card. Play it only if you're short.
Matzalantli, the Great Door: Trap rare — 50.0% GIH and 47.3% OH from a three-mana artifact whose only immediate effect is a rummage. The flip needs four permanent types in your graveyard, which is real work for a mana land. 38.8% play rate is the correct read: leave it in the sideboard outside dedicated UB descend.
The Millennium Calendar: Unplayable. 40.5% with -8.0 IWD is the worst number you'll see in LCI — it does nothing to the board, ever, and the thousand-life clause will not happen in a draft game. Leave it in the sideboard even in a deck short on playables.
Roaming Throne: First-pickable colorless beater, though not a bomb. A four-mana 4/4 with ward 2 dodges most of the format's cheap interaction and stabilizes any deck at any table — the 97.2% play rate and 1.3 ALSA mean it's a zero-risk pick. The tribal doubling is upside you'll rarely need.
Scampering Surveyor: Solid colourless glue at 57.1% GIH — a real 3/2 body attached to the Cave/splash engine, which is how you cash in an off-colour bomb for almost nothing. Every caves or control deck wants one; aggressive RW decks can skip it.
Sorcerous Spyglass: Effectively unplayable — a 0.2% play rate and no win-rate data at all. Two mana for a hand peek and a named activated-ability lock answers almost nothing in a format whose threats are creatures and combat. Sideboard filler only; this read is from the text, not from games.
Sunbird Standard: Role-player that earns its slot by unlocking splashes — fix a bomb off a hidden land, then craft it into a multicolor flyer when the board stalls. 54.0% on a 33.5% play rate reads as a card that's good when you need it and dead when you don't. Never an early pick.
Swashbuckler's Whip: Sideboard — 48.4% and a 6.4% play rate, the clearest cut in the chunk. One mana for reach plus a {2}-tap ability sounds like soft removal, but it costs you a card, an equip, and a creature's attack each turn, and the Discover 10 mode is fantasy. Only bring it in against a heavy flyers deck.
Tarrian's Soulcleaver: Overdrafted rare — a 2.0 ALSA against a 52.9% GIH means players take it far earlier than it deserves. One mana plus two to equip for vigilance and slow counters is too passive; it only shines in a BR/BG board that's actually trading every turn. Late playable, never a first pick.
Threefold Thunderhulk: Take it, but it's a finisher, not a slam. 56.9% GIH with a 94% play rate and 1.3 ALSA — it's colorless so every deck plays it — yet drawn WR (58.5%) well above opening (54.5%) says it's a card you want on turn seven, not turn one. It wins the game if it attacks once.
Throne of the Grim Captain: Archetype-conditional but worth speculating on — the two-mana front is a self-mill engine for UB/BG descend, and the flip ends games outright. LCI's tribes are spread widely enough that assembling Dino/Merfolk/Pirate/Vampire is doable by the late game. The 58.8% GIH and +11.7 IWD are conditioned on decks that could actually craft it; a 39% play rate says plenty couldn't.
Treasure Map: Overdrafted — the data disagrees with Kenji here. A 2.0 ALSA against a 51.5% GIH and a negative IWD means players take it far higher than it performs: three activations before it flips is slow, and scry 1 doesn't affect the board in a format where you cannot be the deck with no early plays. Fine in a true control or splash-heavy build; not the early pick its ALSA suggests.
Captivating Cave: Free inclusion in nearly any deck — it fixes a splash, counts as a cave for the payoffs and converts to two counters when you flood. 55.3% at an 81.1% play rate is exactly what a no-cost land looks like. Not a pick to prioritize, but exactly the tool that makes taking an off-colour bomb nearly free.
Cavern of Souls: Near-unplayable in Limited — 51.4% and a 33.5% play rate for a land that adds colorless unless you're casting one creature type. Your deck isn't tribal enough to matter, and the fixing is worse than a basic in a two-color deck. It's a $100 card, not a playable; ship it.
Cavernous Maw: Only for a genuine cave deck with 5-7 Caves and a Compass Gnome to find them. As a colorless land it costs your mana base something, and the 3/3 needs three Caves before it turns on. 53.2% at 31.2% play — a tool for the control builds, never a pick over a spell.
Echoing Deeps: Near-unplayable rare. Most games it's a tapped colorless Cave, because a useful nonbasic in a graveyard is not something you can plan around. Only run it if you're at 6+ caves and actively want the Cave type; otherwise the 49.5% is generous.
Forgotten Monument: Take it if you have 5-7 Caves — it converts them all into any-colour sources, which is what makes a free splash for a bomb legal. The +5.1 IWD is fixing, not power. In a two-colour deck with two Caves it's a colourless land doing nothing.
Hidden Cataract: Free roll in any blue deck. It costs you a tapped land early and hands you Discover 4 once the game goes long, which is exactly the mana-sink the control and caves decks want. 80% play rate at 55.4% — take it late, run 18 lands with it, don't count it as a spell.
Hidden Courtyard: Free inclusion in any white deck — it costs you a tapped land and gives control and descend builds a real mana sink that discovers into a four-drop. 79.4% play rate at 55.3% is the whole story. Run one or two; more than that and the tapped lands cost you the RW aggro starts.
Hidden Necropolis: Free-roll land for any black deck — 55.2% and 78% play rate on effectively zero cost beyond entering tapped. Late game it cashes in for Discover 4, which is a real card plus tempo. Count it toward your 17-18 and toward cave payoffs; take it whenever the pack is otherwise empty.
Hidden Nursery: Free inclusion in any green deck — a tapped land is a small cost for a late-game discover 4 mana sink, and it counts toward the cave payoffs. The 55.5% is mostly the decks playing it being fine; run one or two, never spend a real pick on it.
Hidden Volcano: Free inclusion in any red deck. Enters tapped is a real cost in a format where you never want to be the deck with no early plays, but the late-game discover 4 is genuine value off a land slot. Run one or two; you don't need to force a 'caves deck' to justify it.
Pit of Offerings: Playable only as a cave-count enabler with a relevant fixing mode, never as a good land. It enters tapped and the graveyard exile is usually irrelevant — 46.4% opening-hand WR is the cost of tapping out on a key turn. Run it in an 18-land control deck that needs caves or a splash, cut it from anything aggressive.
Promising Vein: Run exactly one in a two-color deck that wants caves. The extra mana on the activation is genuinely too slow to fix on curve, so treat it as a colorless land that turns into the right basic later plus a cave count for Bat Colony or Gargantuan Leech. 53.6% GIH is a land doing land things — never a real pick, just a late-pack freeroll.
Restless Anchorage: High pick in WU and a genuine reason to be in the best pair — a colourless-cost land that becomes a 2/3 flyer, breaks board stalls the way the doctrine says stalls break, and makes Map tokens for your artifact and explore payoffs. 59.2% with +4.5 IWD, and it costs you nothing but a tapped land.
Restless Prairie: Good in GW, unplayable outside it — a free late-game threat on a land slot that also pumps your team when it attacks, which is exactly what the underdrafted 55.45% Selesnya go-wide deck wants. 56.6% with +3.5 IWD. The enters-tapped cost is real for aggro, so don't run two.
Restless Reef: Best of the manlands here and near-free to run in UB. 57.3% with +7.1 IWD off a land slot is great value: a 4/4 deathtouch attacker that mills you toward descend thresholds while dodging sorcery removal. The enters-tapped and four-mana activation keep it honest.
Restless Ridgeline: Effectively a free win condition for RG — a land that becomes a 3/4 and untaps a second attacker with a pump on top. Entering tapped is the whole cost. The 62.1% opening-hand WR is genuine, but it's RG-conditional: the 65.9% play rate is just how often drafters land in those colors.
Restless Vents: Effectively a free roll for BR: it enters tapped but costs no card, threatens as a menace attacker with built-in looting that also feeds descend. 55.1% GIH. The catch is it only goes in the format's worst pair — don't treat it as a reason to be there.
Sunken Citadel: Narrow — only for a deck built on land abilities, and note LoL's blurb describes a different cave; this one makes mana usable solely for land activations, not colour fixing. With several caves and Discover lands it's a genuine accelerant, otherwise it's a tapped land that casts nothing.
Volatile Fault: Don't play it. 48.9% GIH with a 46.4% opening-hand WR: a colorless land in a format with heavy double-pip costs, and the Strip Mine mode mostly hands the opponent a basic while fixing nothing. Only worth a slot if you're desperate for a Treasure to power a splash.
Deeproot Pilgrimage: Trap rare at 46.6% — the worst number here. LCI has nowhere near the Merfolk density to turn a two-mana do-nothing enchantment into a token engine, and tapping to attack means the tokens arrive after you've already committed. Sideboard; play a creature instead.
Subterranean Schooner: Premium blue rare and a top-tier two-drop: crew 1 means a single Map or one-drop turns it on, and a 3/4 attacker that explores each swing snowballs fast. 66.6% opening-hand WR — the earliest you deploy it, the better. Core WU/UR pick.
Acolyte of Aclazotz: Don't play it — the data buries LoL's read. 47.8% GIH and 26% play rate is the floor of this chunk: a 1/4 that taps to drain for one is far too slow, and the BR sacrifice shell it enables is the worst pair in the format at 52.48%. Tokens don't fuel descend either.
Bloodletter of Aclazotz: Bomb in a heavy-black deck, but the {1}{B}{B}{B} cost means you cannot splash it. A 2/4 flier alone blanks the format's cheap evasion, and the doubling turns any burn spell, drain, or attack into a fast clock. +6.2 IWD at ALSA 1.7; take it first and commit to black rather than treating it as a late splash.
Defossilize: Strong black uncommon, pick it in the top half of a pack. Five mana to reanimate your best creature with two explores attached is a swing that ends grindy games, and +6.5 IWD backs it up. It wants a self-mill or land-cycling shell (BG, UB, Jund); in a pure aggro deck it's too slow, as Numot notes.
Fungal Fortitude: Playable trick in a grindy black deck, not a maindeck staple — flash plus +2/+0 wins a combat and the creature comes back, which is genuine two-for-one value in BG/UB attrition. But 19.9% play rate and a 51.5% OH say it's slow and situational. Take it late; it's a good answer to targeted removal in a deck with one key creature.
Souls of the Lost: Strong in committed BG/UB self-mill, a liability elsewhere — the additional cost means an early copy is a 1/2 that ate a card, and 52.8% OH vs 59.1% GD is the sharpest split in the chunk. Late it's a two-mana 6/7. Draft it once you have Another Chance and Death-Cap Marionette, not before.
Cosmium Confluence: Archetype-conditional payoff, not a slam. Five mana that does nothing without Caves already in play, and GD 57.3% against OH 51.8% confirms it's a late-game card. Fine in a green control build with 6+ Caves; unplayable in the RG beatdown deck green usually ends up in.
Chimil, the Inner Sun: Bomb, full stop — the best card in this group and a P1P1 in any deck since it's colorless. Six mana for a permanent that free-casts a spell every end step ends the game in two turns, and nothing in the set's common interaction answers an artifact. The +8.2 IWD is the real thing.
Runaway Boulder: Low-end playable that shines because of cycling — six mana for six damage at flash speed is overpriced, but a removal spell that becomes a card when it's too slow has no downside. 52.6% GIH, 17% play: last two slots in a slower deck.
